client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just... can't bring myself to go, because being around everyone just makes her absence feel even more overwhelming. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step to reach out — even when part of you isn't sure it will help, showing up like this takes real courage, and I want you to know that matters. The grief you're carrying sounds very heavy, and it makes a lot of sense that being around family right now amplifies the pain of her absence rather than easing it. I'd gently invite you to notice that avoiding those gatherings, while understandable, might be quietly reinforcing the belief that you can't cope with that pain — and together, we can explore whether there might be small, manageable ways to reconnect without feeling so overwhelmed.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, but I'm not sure avoiding the gatherings is really about not being able to cope — it's more that being there feels like a constant reminder that she's just... gone, and everyone else seems to be moving on like it's normal. It's like I'd be sitting there pretending everything is fine when it really isn't. I don't know if "small, manageable steps" is the right framing for something that feels this big.
therapist: You're right to push back on that, and I hear you — this isn't about coping ability, it's about the unbearable feeling of being surrounded by people who seem to have resumed normal life while you're still sitting with a loss that feels anything but normal. The way you're speaking, quickly and softly, almost like the words are tumbling out under pressure, tells me this is something you've been holding very tightly inside. That sense of having to pretend — to perform "fine" when you're not — is its own kind of exhausting, and I think that deserves to be the real starting point for us, rather than rushing toward steps or solutions.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, that's... that's exactly it. I've been holding it so tight that sometimes I forget I'm even doing it, and then I'll be in the middle of a conversation with a coworker or something and I realize I'm just performing, like I'm watching myself from outside, saying the right things and nodding at the right moments. And then I go home and I just feel this hollow exhaustion, like I spent the whole day being someone I'm not.
therapist: What you're describing — that dissociation of watching yourself perform from the outside — is a really significant thing to name, and the fact that your voice carries this kind of stretched, almost suspended quality as you say it makes me think part of you is still mid-performance even right now, still monitoring yourself carefully. That hollow exhaustion you feel at the end of the day makes complete sense, because maintaining that mask takes an enormous amount of energy that grief is already stealing from you. I'm wondering — in this space, right now, what would it feel like to not have to perform, even just for a few minutes?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I actually don't know what that would feel like — and that's kind of terrifying to admit, because I think I've been performing for so long that I'm not sure there's anything underneath it anymore. Like, what if I stop and there's just... nothing there? Not grief, not relief, just emptiness. That scares me more than the exhaustion does, honestly.
therapist: The fear in what you just said is palpable — and yet the way you're speaking, with this rapid, almost breathless quality, tells me that what's underneath isn't nothing, it's actually something quite alive and frightened, which is the opposite of emptiness. That terror of finding a void is one of the most common and painful fears in grief, but in CBT terms it's worth gently questioning the thought itself — because the very fact that the idea of "nothing" scares you so much is evidence that there *is* something there that cares deeply. You haven't performed your way out of yourself; you've just buried someone who matters under layers of protection, and she's still there.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but another part of me is just... skeptical, I guess. Like, it sounds nice in theory that there's still something there underneath all of this, but what if that's just something therapists say to make people feel better? I've been going through the motions for so long that I honestly can't tell anymore whether I'm feeling genuine grief or just performing what grief is supposed to look like.
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid, and I want to be clear — I'm not saying it to make you feel better, I'm saying it because you've shown me the evidence yourself in this very conversation. The fact that you can't tell whether your grief is "real" or performed is itself one of the most disorienting parts of prolonged grief, and that confusion doesn't mean the feeling isn't genuine — it means you've been disconnected from yourself for a long time. What if, instead of trying to decide whether your grief is real, we just got curious about what's actually present in you right now, without needing to label or justify it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess that makes sense, but I'm not sure I even know how to do that — just "get curious" without judging what I find. Every time I try to sit with what I'm feeling, I end up either going numb or spiraling into this guilt about whether I even have the right to grieve him the way I do. It's like my brain won't let me just... be in it without turning it into some kind of trial.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, with this high, almost tightly wound quality — tells me your mind is working really hard to stay in control even as you're describing the exact thing that takes control away from you, and that tension between wanting to feel and needing to manage is exhausting. That guilt about whether you have the "right" to grieve is something I really want to sit with you on, because that word — *right* — suggests there's some internal judge putting your grief on trial before it's even allowed to exist. Can we gently ask together: where did you learn that your grief needed to be earned or justified before it was allowed to be real?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hadn't really thought about it that way before — that there's like a judge inside me deciding if my grief counts. But honestly, when you say "where did you learn that," I almost want to laugh, because it feels so obvious now... my family never really made space for that kind of thing. If you weren't visibly falling apart over something "serious enough," you just got on with it, and I guess I internalized that more than I realized.
therapist: That almost-laugh you mentioned is really important — it's the sound of something clicking into place, a moment of genuine recognition rather than performance, and that's actually you connecting with yourself, not watching from the outside. What you've just uncovered is significant: you didn't develop this inner judge randomly, you inherited a family rule that grief had to be *serious enough* to deserve space, and you've been applying that rule to yourself ever since — essentially doing to yourself what your family did to the room. The fact that your voice carries this bright, quick, almost surprised energy right now tells me this realization is landing somewhere real in you, not just intellectually but somewhere deeper.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I mean... I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to just accept it and feel better, but there's another part that's already pulling back and going "okay but so what, now what." Like, understanding where the rule came from doesn't automatically make me stop enforcing it on myself, you know? It's like knowing why a door is stuck doesn't suddenly make it open.
therapist: Your door metaphor is exactly right, and I don't want to pretend that insight alone is the key — understanding the rule is just the beginning, not the finish line. But I notice something in how you're speaking right now — there's this high, quick, almost braced quality, like part of you is already preparing to be disappointed by this process, which makes me wonder if that same inner judge is in the room right now, already deciding that understanding won't be "enough." The work of actually loosening that rule happens slowly, through small moments of choosing to let your grief exist without putting it on trial — and you've already done that, quietly, several times in this conversation today.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, you're probably right that I'm already bracing for disappointment — I do that a lot, actually, like I'm trying to get ahead of the letdown before it hits me. But when you say I've already done it "several times today," I honestly don't know what moments you're referring to, and part of me wonders if you're just saying that to make me feel better. I want to believe it's real progress, but it feels too small and too quiet to count for anything.
therapist: I hear the skepticism, and I want to be specific rather than vague: you let your grief exist without justifying it when you named the hollow exhaustion, when you admitted you didn't know what it felt like to stop performing, when you laughed with recognition instead of deflecting — those were real moments of dropping the trial, even briefly. And the way you're speaking right now, very fast and high, almost like you're rushing to disqualify things before they can matter, is that same bracing pattern in action — your judge is in here with us, trying to rule those moments "too small to count" before you can let them land. But "small and quiet" is exactly what real progress feels like when you've spent years expecting yourself to either fall apart dramatically or feel nothing — it doesn't announce itself, it just quietly refuses to perform.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hate that you just described me that way because it's accurate and I didn't want it to be. The rushing thing, the disqualifying before things can matter, I felt myself doing it even as you were talking and I couldn't stop it. It's like there's this part of me that's genuinely terrified of what happens if I let something small actually count, like maybe it means I have to admit I've been wrong about myself for a long time.
therapist: That moment of "I hate that it's accurate" — that's not resistance, that's honesty, and it's one of the most courageous things a person can say in this room. Your voice carries something that sounds almost like it's stretched taut right now, like you're holding something very carefully that you're afraid to put down, and I think you've just named the real heart of all of this: that letting something small count means confronting the possibility that you've been holding yourself to a false story for a very long time. That's not something to rush past — that's the door, and you're standing right in front of it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
